s: King Lemuel is a king whose mother taught him a revelation. She addresses him as son of her womb and vows, warning against giving strength to women or drinking wine, and urging righteous judgment and justice for the poor and needy.

King Lemuel's mother teaches him a revelation, addressing him tenderly as her son, the son of her womb and of her vows. She warns him against giving his strength to women and against kings' drinking, and charges him to speak for the mute and judge righteously for the poor and needy.

l: worthy woman (the woman of Proverbs 31), Proverbs
s: The worthy woman is described as far more valuable than rubies. She works wool and flax, buys a field and plants a vineyard, rises at night to feed her household and servant girls, sells linen garments and sashes, opens her hands to the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kind instruction. She is clothed in strength and dignity, laughs at the time to come, and is praised by her children and husband, with the conclusion that a woman who fears the LORD shall be praised and her works should praise her in the gates.

The worthy woman's husband trusts her with his heart and will have no lack of gain, as she does him good and not harm all her days. He is respected in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land, and he praises her by saying many women do noble things but she excels them all.

In Lemuel's mother's instruction, the poor and needy are those for whom the king must open his mouth and serve justice, along with the mute and the desolate. The worthy woman opens her arms and extends her hands to them.
Justice is something kings risk perverting for the afflicted if they drink wine and forget the law. Lemuel is told to judge righteously and serve justice to the poor and needy.

The Book of Hosea, in fourteen chapters, is a prophetic text in which the LORD accuses Israel of unfaithfulness, announces judgment, and ends by promising restoration. Its central figures are the LORD, Hosea son of Beeri, his wife Gomer, and the people addressed as Israel, Ephraim, Samaria and Judah. Chapter 1 opens with the LORD commanding Hosea to take a wife of prostitution because the land has forsaken him. Gomer bears three children named Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah and Lo-Ammi, names that signal judgment on Israel. Mercy for Judah and a future united, countless people are promised. Chapter 2 develops the image of an unfaithful mother who credits her lovers and Baal with the LORD's gifts. He will strip her and end her feasts, then allure her into the wilderness, betroth her to himself forever, and show mercy to those once called 'not my people'. Chapter 3 has the speaker buy back an adulteress as the LORD loves Israel despite its other gods; Israel will live long without king or sacrifice, then return to seek the LORD and David their king. Chapters 4 through 8 present the charge. There is no truth, goodness or knowledge of God, and the land mourns. Priests, princes and kings are condemned for idolatry, prostitution, scheming and rebellion against the covenant. Ephraim turns to Assyria and Egypt instead of the LORD, and in chapter 6 the LORD says he desires mercy and knowledge of God more than sacrifice. Israel sows the wind and will reap the whirlwind, and Samaria's calf idol will be broken. Chapters 9 through 13 deepen the judgment. Israel will lose harvest, land and children and be scattered. Its altars and calves will be demolished, and its king will be destroyed. Chapter 11 recalls the LORD loving Israel as a child and teaching Ephraim to walk. His compassion is aroused, and he will not destroy Ephraim, for he is God and not man. Chapter 12 recalls Jacob and condemns Ephraim's dishonest wealth. Chapter 13 compares the LORD to a lion, leopard and bear and ends with Samaria falling by the sword. Chapter 14 closes with a call to return, supplies words of repentance and renounces Assyria, horses and idols. The LORD promises to heal and love them freely, to be like dew so Israel blossoms, and the book ends by asking who is wise enough to see that his ways are right.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea
s: The LORD is the divine speaker throughout the Book of Hosea, presented as God of Israel since the land of Egypt, the God of Armies, the Holy One, and Israel's only savior. He is portrayed through a marriage metaphor: husband to an unfaithful mother (Israel), who gave her grain, wine, oil, silver and gold, yet she turned to other gods. The central tension is between his judgment and his enduring love. The records open with commands to Hosea to take an unfaithful wife and name children as signs of judgment: no mercy on Israel, mercy on Judah, and a promise that Israel's children will be countless and gathered under one head. He declares he is no longer husband to the unfaithful mother, punishes her, then promises to allure her into the wilderness, betroth her forever in righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion and faithfulness, and call those who were not his people 'my people.' He loves Israel as a picture of loving an adulteress. He then charges the land with lacking truth, goodness and knowledge of God, rejects the priests, and knows Ephraim. He is figuratively a moth to Ephraim and rottenness to Judah, withdraws from those seeking him with sacrifices, and will be a lion tearing them. He desires mercy and knowledge of God over sacrifice, accuses them of breaking his covenant and law, wishes to heal and redeem Israel though they lie against him, remembers their wickedness, spreads his net, rejects their offerings, is angry at Samaria's calf idol, hates Gilgal, and will destroy altars and sacred stones, drive Israel out and chastise them. Yet he recalls loving Israel as a child, calling his son out of Egypt, teaching Ephraim to walk, and feeding him with cords of love. His compassion is aroused and he will not destroy Ephraim, for he is God and not man; he will settle them in their houses. Later he punishes Jacob by his deeds, reminds them he spoke through prophets, and as lion, leopard and bear sends an east wind to dry up Ephraim. The records end with a call to return: he will heal their waywardness, love them freely, turn his anger away, be like dew and a green cypress, show mercy to the fatherless, and his ways are right.
Hosea, son of Beeri, receives the LORD's word during the reigns of Judah's kings and Jeroboam of Israel, obeys the command to marry Gomer, and fathers three children whom he names as directed.

Judah is the people or house of Judah, addressed in the Book of Hosea during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. It begins with a promise of mercy: the LORD will save it not by weapons but by himself, and its children will later be gathered with Israel's under one head. Chapter 5 turns to warning: Judah stumbles with Israel and Ephraim, its princes are like those who remove a landmark, and the LORD's wrath and a lion's tearing await it. Chapter 6 laments its fleeting love, like morning cloud and dew, yet promises an appointed harvest when the LORD restores his people's fortunes.

Israel is the LORD's people, addressed throughout the Book of Hosea as a nation, a house, and a son, and it is the subject of an extended indictment followed by a promise of restoration. It is closely tied to Ephraim, which is joined to idols, and is often named alongside Judah. The records open under king Jeroboam son of Joash, with judgment: the land commits great adultery by forsaking the LORD, its kingdom will cease, its bow will be broken in Jezreel, and mercy will end. A future promise is set beside this, that its children will be as countless as the sand of the sea, be called sons of the living God, and be united with Judah under one head. The central charge is unfaithfulness. Israel is stubborn like a heifer, led astray by a spirit of prostitution, and a covenant breaker. It consults a wooden idol, worships at high places under oaks, poplars and terebinths, makes idols of silver and gold, and multiplies altars and sacred stones as its land prospers. It sacrifices to the Baals and burns incense to engraved images. Its pride testifies against it, it is defiled yet not hidden from the LORD, and its heart is divided. It set up kings and princes without the LORD's approval, forgot its Maker while building palaces, and sought Assyria like a wild donkey. It trusts its own way and mighty men and refuses to repent. Its sin is traced back to Gibeah and Baal Peor. The account unfolds from judgment to restoration. The middle chapters show the people refusing to return, being swallowed up among the nations like a worthless thing, losing harvest and land, returning to Egypt, and facing fire on its cities, fallen fortresses, and a king destroyed. The LORD recalls loving Israel as a child called out of Egypt and hesitates to abandon it like Admah and Zeboiim. Chapter 13 says Israel is destroyed because it is against the LORD, its helper. The final chapter calls it to return, gives it words asking forgiveness and renouncing Assyria, horses, and handmade gods, and promises that it will blossom like the lily, root and have fragrance like Lebanon, and have beauty like the olive tree.
is_daughter_of Diblaim Gomer the daughter of Diblaim is taken as wife by Hosea at the LORD's command. She bears a son, then a daughter, and after weaning the daughter bears another son.

l: Jezreel (Hosea's son), The Book of Hosea
s: Jezreel is the first son of Hosea and Gomer, named at the LORD's instruction. His name signals judgment: the LORD will avenge Jezreel's blood on Jehu's house, end Israel's kingdom, and break its bow in the valley, yet great will be Jezreel's day.
Lo-Ruhamah is Gomer's second child, a daughter born after Jezreel. The LORD names her to signify no more mercy for the house of Israel. She is weaned before her brother is conceived.
Lo-Ammi is a son born to Gomer after Lo-Ruhamah was weaned. His LORD-given name, 'not my people,' signals Israel's rejection, yet the LORD later promises they will be called 'sons of the living God.'

l: mother (Israel, the unfaithful wife), The Book of Hosea
s: The mother is accused of prostitution and of going after her lovers, whom she credited with her bread, water, wool, flax, oil and drink, not knowing the LORD gave them. She will chase her lovers without success, and be stripped and stripped of her gifts, then be allured into the wilderness, where she will respond as in her youth and be betrothed to the LORD forever.

l: children (Israel's children), The Book of Hosea
s: The children are told to say 'My people' and 'My loved one' to their brothers and sisters, and to contend with their mother. The LORD says he will have no mercy on them because they are children of unfaithfulness.

l: lovers (of the mother), The Book of Hosea
s: The lovers are the ones the mother follows, believing they give her food, drink, wool, flax and oil. She will not overtake them or find them, and her lewdness will be uncovered in their sight, with no one able to deliver her from the LORD's hand.

The silver and gold the LORD multiplied for the mother were used for Baal, and she burned incense to the Baals in the days that the LORD will visit on her. The LORD promises to take the names of the Baals out of her mouth so they are no longer mentioned.

Egypt is a place that recurs as refuge, derision, and origin. Ephraim, easily deceived, calls to it for help, and its derision awaits fallen princes. Ephraim will return there, and Memphis will bury the fleeing. Israel was called out of it, and the people will finally come trembling like a bird from it.

l: betrothal (of the LORD to his people), The Book of Hosea
s: The LORD promises to betroth the people to himself forever, in righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion and faithfulness, so that they shall know the LORD. In that day she will call him 'my husband' and not 'my master', and those who were 'not my people' will be called his people.

l: unfaithfulness and prostitution, The Book of Hosea
s: The mother's prostitution and adulteries are the charge at the center of the chapter, and her children are called children of unfaithfulness. She is told to put them away from her face and from between her breasts, and the LORD's judgment, including stripping, wilderness and the loss of his gifts, answers them.

l: woman (loved by another, bought by the speaker), The Book of Hosea
s: A woman loved by another man and called an adulteress is bought by the speaker for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley. He tells her to stay with him many days, not to prostitute herself or belong to any other man, and promises to be faithful toward her.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Hosea
s: The children of Israel are loved by the LORD despite turning to other gods and loving cakes of raisins. They will live many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod or idols, and afterward return, seeking the LORD their God and David their king.

l: idols (wooden idol), The Book of Hosea
s: The people consult their wooden idol and answer to a stick of wood, led astray by a spirit of prostitution. They sacrifice and burn incense on mountaintops and hills under shady trees, and Ephraim is said to be joined to idols.

l: Israel's return to the LORD in the last days, The Book of Hosea
s: After many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod or idols, the children of Israel afterward return and seek the LORD their God and David their king, coming with trembling to the LORD and his blessings in the last days.

Ephraim is a figurative name for a people, closely tied to Israel, whom the LORD addresses, accuses and judges across these records. The dominant theme is unfaithfulness: Ephraim is joined to idols, likened to a prostitute, defiled, and said to have made molten images from its silver. Its love for the LORD is like a morning cloud or early-vanishing dew, and it has not returned to him despite pride testifying against it. Chapter 5 opens with Ephraim known to the LORD, stumbling in iniquity, oppressed and crushed in judgment. Seeing its sickness, it turns to Assyria, which cannot heal it. Chapter 7 deepens the picture: Ephraim mixes among the nations, is like an unturned pancake and a burning oven, and is a dove easily deceived and without understanding, calling to Egypt and going to Assyria while strangers devour its strength and gray hairs go unnoticed. It is also a faulty bow, returning but not to the Most High. Later chapters turn to coming judgment. Planted like Tyre in a pleasant place, it will nonetheless return to Egypt, be barren, see its children given to the murderer, have its root dried up, and wander among the nations. It is a trained heifer who loves to thresh, and it will receive shame. It feeds on wind, chases the east wind, multiplies lies and desolation, covenants with Assyria, sends oil to Egypt, and boasts of wealth while denying iniquity. It has provoked the LORD bitterly, so its blood stays on it. Once exalted in Israel, it died through Baal, its guilt is stored up, and it is an unwise son who fails to come to the opening of the womb, though fruitful among its brothers. Yet mercy runs alongside judgment. The LORD taught Ephraim to walk and healed it unrecognized, asks how he can give it up, and says he will not execute his fierce anger or destroy it. The story ends with the LORD asking what Ephraim has to do with idols any more, and promising to answer and care for it, with its fruit found in him.

l: inhabitants of the land (Israel), The Book of Hosea
s: The land's inhabitants lack knowledge of God, truth and goodness; the LORD charges them with cursing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery and bloodshed, and they are destroyed, practicing prostitution and idolatry, ruined without understanding.

l: land (Israel's land), The Book of Hosea
s: will_suffer mourning and wasting away [consequence of the people's sin] The land will mourn because of the people's sins, and everyone who dwells in it will waste away. The animals of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea will also die.

The priests are a group accused of rejecting knowledge and God's law, so the LORD rejects them and forgets their children. They feed on the people's sin and set their hearts on iniquity, so they will be punished like the people, and are called a snare at Mizpah.

l: sins and moral corruption, The Book of Hosea
s: The chapter lists cursing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery, breaking boundaries, bloodshed, prostitution, and drunkenness as the people's sins. These increased as the people multiplied, take away understanding, and bring the LORD's punishment, the land's mourning, and the people's ruin.

Assyria is a foreign power Ephraim turns to, like a senseless dove, and the LORD will net them; it becomes Israel's king after refusal to repent, yet later the returning people come trembling from it and are resettled.

l: spirit of prostitution, The Book of Hosea
s: dwells_in Israel [prevents them from turning to God] The spirit of prostitution is said to be within the people, so that their deeds will not allow them to turn to their God. It accompanies their not knowing the LORD.

is_against priests [also house of Israel and house of the king] Judgment is declared against the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king, who have been a snare at Mizpah and a net on Tabor. Ephraim is crushed in judgment, and the day of rebuke will make it a desolation.

l: mercy and knowledge of God over sacrifice, The Book of Hosea
s: The LORD states that He desires mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. This is set against the people's fleeting love, their covenant-breaking like Adam, and the violence and shameful crimes described in Gilead and on the path toward Shechem.

l: return and restoration, The Book of Hosea
s: The chapter begins with a call to return to the LORD, trusting that He will heal, bind wounds, revive on the third day, and come like the rain, and urging the people to press on to know Him. It ends with the LORD's statement that a harvest is appointed for Judah when He restores the fortunes of His people.

Samaria is a place with a king, whose people rebel against the LORD, their God. It begins with a command to discard its calf idol, which is called a workman's creation and will be broken. It then faces terror over the calves, with its king floating away like a twig, and ends bearing guilt through violent destruction by the sword.

l: wickedness and falsehood of the people, The Book of Hosea
s: pleases the king [also the princes] The people commit falsehood, with thieves entering and robber gangs ravaging, and they gladden the king and princes with wickedness and lies. Their hearts burn like an oven with adultery, drunkenness, mockery, and smoldering anger, and they devour their judges. They do not cry to the LORD with their heart, plot evil against him, and speak lies against him, and their deeds have engulfed them.

l: molten images and idols (Ephraim's idols), The Book of Hosea
s: Ephraim's molten images and idols, including the Samaria calf, are craftsmen's silver works declared no God; people sacrifice to and kiss the calves, while the LORD's anger burns and they will be broken in pieces.

l: altars (Ephraim's altars), The Book of Hosea
s: Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning, and these altars became for him altars for sinning. The LORD does not accept the sacrifices offered there, and he will remember and punish the iniquity.

l: unfaithfulness and idolatry, The Book of Hosea
s: Israel's unfaithfulness is likened to loving a prostitute's wages at every threshing floor. Their corruption is compared to the days of Gibeah, and at Baal Peor they consecrated themselves to the shameful thing and became abominable like what they loved. All their wickedness is said to be in Gilgal, and their princes are rebels.

l: coming judgment, The Book of Hosea
s: is_for Israel [days of visitation and reckoning] The days of visitation and reckoning are declared to have come. Judgment includes failed harvests, exile to Egypt and Assyria, polluted food, rejected offerings, nettles and thorns in their homes, and being driven from the LORD's house. It ends with God casting them away so that they become wanderers among the nations.

l: barrenness and childlessness, The Book of Hosea
s: Ephraim's judgment is described as no birth, no pregnancy and no conception, and even raised children will be taken so that no man is left. The prophet asks the LORD to give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts. Even if they give birth, the LORD says he will kill the beloved ones of their womb.

l: calves of Beth Aven, The Book of Hosea
s: Idol calves located in Beth Aven terrify Samaria's inhabitants; people and priests mourn their departed glory, and the calf will finally be carried to Assyria as tribute to a great king.

Jacob is an individual recalled as grasping his brother's heel in the womb, then contending with God and an angel as an adult and prevailing. He wept, found God at Bethel, fled to Aram, and served tending flocks to win a wife, and is to be repaid per his deeds.

l: altars (of Israel), The Book of Hosea
s: Israel multiplied its altars in proportion to the abundance of its fruit. The LORD will demolish them, and the thorn and thistle will come up on them.

l: sacred stones (of Israel), The Book of Hosea
s: Israel adorned its sacred stones as its land prospered. The LORD will destroy them.

l: judgment against Israel, The Book of Hosea
s: has_form poisonous weeds in furrows [simile] Judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field because of false promises and covenants. It includes shame, destroyed high places, a battle roar, ruined fortresses as at Beth Arbel, and the destruction of Israel's king at daybreak, with nations gathered against the people.

l: sin and wickedness, The Book of Hosea
s: has_result judgment springs up like poisonous weeds [consequence of false covenants] Israel's sin includes divided loyalty, swearing falsely in covenants, multiplying altars, and persisting in wrongdoing since Gibeah. The people have plowed wickedness, reaped iniquity, and eaten the fruit of lies by trusting in their own way and mighty men.

l: wealth and deceit of Ephraim, The Book of Hosea
s: is_a claim of wealth without sin [Ephraim's boast] A merchant with dishonest scales in his hand loves to defraud, and Ephraim says he has become rich and found himself wealth. He claims that in all his wealth no iniquity that is sin will be found in him. The LORD answers that he will make them dwell in tents again, and that Ephraim's provocation will bring his blood upon him.

l: king (Israel's king), The Book of Hosea
s: The LORD asks where Israel's king is now to save them in all their cities, recalling that the people asked for a king and princes. He says he gave a king in his anger and took him away in his wrath.

l: Israel's judgment and destruction, The Book of Hosea
s: A prophecy of Samaria's doom: the people vanish like mist, dew, chaff and smoke; the LORD ambushes them like a lion, leopard and bear, sends a drying east wind, and the sword brings slaughter.
is_a work of human hands The people are to stop calling the work of their hands 'Our gods.' The LORD asks Ephraim what he has to do any more with idols.
Sin is named as the reason Israel has fallen. Israel is to ask the LORD to forgive all their sins, and the LORD responds by promising to heal their waywardness and turn away his anger.

The Book of Amos, as presented in these nine chapters, is a prophetic text of judgment attributed to Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa, who saw his words concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, two years before the earthquake. The LORD, who roars from Zion, is the central figure; Israel, especially its elites, and the nations around it are the main subjects. Chapters 1 and 2 open with judgments, each introduced by 'for three transgressions, yes, for four,' on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and Judah. Each nation is charged with specific wrongs and threatened with fire on its palaces. The longest section targets Israel for selling the righteous and needy, trampling the poor, and silencing prophets, despite the LORD having brought them out of Egypt. Chapters 3 to 6 develop the case against Israel. Because the LORD chose Israel alone, he will punish it. Rhetorical questions argue that disaster has a cause and that the LORD reveals his plans to the prophets. Samaria's oppression, the 'cows of Bashan,' and empty worship at Bethel and Gilgal are condemned. A list of calamities is each followed by the refrain that Israel has not returned to him. The text laments Israel's fall, urges people to seek the LORD and live, calls for justice to roll on like rivers, warns that the day of the LORD will be darkness, and pronounces woe on the complacent who lounge on ivory beds while Joseph is afflicted. Captivity beyond Damascus and a nation raised against Israel are announced. Chapters 7 and 8 shift to visions. Locusts and fire are averted when Amos pleads for Jacob, but a plumb line signals that the LORD will no longer pass by Israel. Amaziah the priest of Bethel tells Amos to flee to Judah, and Amos answers that the LORD took him from herding and farming sycamore figs to prophesy, then pronounces judgment on Amaziah's family. A basket of summer fruit signals that the end has come, with cheating of the poor condemned, mourning replacing feasts, and a famine of hearing the LORD's words. Chapter 9 shows the Lord beside the altar, promising that no sinner will escape, though the house of Jacob will not be utterly destroyed. The book ends with a promise to raise David's fallen tent, restore Israel from captivity, and plant them permanently in their land amid abundant harvests.

Amos is a herdsman and sycamore-fig farmer from Tekoa whom the Lord GOD called to prophesy to Israel during the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, two years before the earthquake. His book opens with the LORD roaring from Zion. He receives visions, twice pleading for small Jacob so the LORD relents. Accused by Amaziah of conspiracy and told to flee to Judah, he denies being a professional prophet, pronounces judgment on Amaziah, and repeats that Israel will go captive. A basket of summer fruit signals the end has come, and he denounces those oppressing the needy.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos
s: The LORD, also called the Lord GOD and the God of Armies, is the sovereign deity who speaks throughout the Book of Amos. He roars from Zion and speaks from Jerusalem, opening with judgments on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab and Judah, with fire to devour palaces. The records stress that he turns his attention most sharply on Israel. He recalls destroying the Amorite, bringing Israel up from Egypt, leading them through the wilderness, raising up prophets and Nazirites, and choosing them alone of all earth's families, and for that reason he will punish all their sins. He reveals his secrets to the prophets before acting. He is presented as creator and ruler: he forms mountains and wind, makes the Pleiades and Orion, turns shadow into morning and day into night, builds his rooms in the heavens, and calls the sea's waters onto the earth. He swears by his holiness and by himself, and abhors the pride of Jacob. He claims to have sent hunger, drought, blight, locusts and plagues, yet Israel did not return, and he calls them to seek him and live. He hates their feasts, offerings and songs, and demands that justice roll on like rivers. He remembers dishonest trade practices and will never forget their works. The account moves toward judgment: cows of Bashan taken away with hooks, strong fortresses suddenly destroyed, captivity beyond Damascus, and a nation raised against Israel. In Amos's visions he relents over the locusts and the fire after Amos pleads, but sets a plumb line, shows the basket of summer fruit, and says he will no longer pass by Israel. He promises a famine of hearing his words and darkness at noon. In the final chapter he stands beside the altar, commanding the striking of the pillars and pursuing the sinful wherever they hide. He notes that he also brought up the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir. The close turns to restoration: he will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, will sift Israel, raise up David's fallen tent, bring the people back from captivity, and plant them permanently in the land he gave them.

Israel is the people of the Lord GOD, called "my people Israel," the children of Israel and the house of Jacob. The records portray a chosen people, brought out of Egypt, led forty years in the wilderness, and given prophets and Nazirites, yet persistently unfaithful. Its transgressions are many: oppressing the poor, selling the righteous and needy for silver and sandals, hoarding plunder in palaces, and lounging on couches and silken cushions in Samaria. It gave Nazirites wine and told prophets not to prophesy. Its worship is hollow: it is sarcastically told to sin at Bethel and Gilgal, boasting of its offerings. Despite hunger, drought, blight, locusts, plague, and the sword, it has not returned to the LORD. The account unfolds from indictment to judgment to partial hope. Early chapters recall the LORD's past acts and announce that Israel will be crushed and punished, with only scraps rescued like a shepherd saving two legs from a lion. It is told to prepare to meet its God. Later a plumb line is set in its midst, its sanctuaries will be laid waste, and captivity is foretold. Amos is sent to prophesy despite Amaziah's opposition. Then comes its declared end: songs become wailing, feasts become mourning, and those swearing by Samaria's sin fall. The final chapter says the sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but the house of Jacob will be sifted among nations without losing a kernel, and promises return from captivity, rebuilt cities, vineyards, gardens, possession of the remnant of Edom, and permanent rooting in its land.
Judah is a land condemned for rejecting the LORD's law and statutes and following ancestral lies; as punishment, the LORD will send fire to devour Jerusalem's palaces.
Jeroboam, son of Joash, is king of Israel; the LORD and Amos prophesy judgment, with the sword against his house and his death.

Damascus, a place in Amos 1, is condemned for threshing Gilead with iron instruments; punishment is unavoidable: fire on Hazael's house and Ben Hadad's palaces, its gate bar broken, and Syria's people exiled to Kir.

has_transgression carrying captive the whole community to Edom [punishment not turned away] Gaza is condemned for carrying away captive the whole community to deliver them up to Edom. The LORD says he will send fire on its wall to devour its palaces, and will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod and the scepter-holder from Ashkelon, turn his hand against Ekron, and cause the remnant of the Philistines to perish.

Edom, a nation with a place (Bozrah) and a people, is condemned in Amos 1 for pursuing his brother with the sword, showing no pity, and nursing perpetual wrath; the LORD vows fire on Teman devouring Bozrah's palaces.
Tyre is a place condemned in Amos 1 for delivering the whole community to Edom and forgetting the brotherly covenant; the LORD vows fire on its wall to devour palaces.

Ammon, the children of Ammon, is condemned for ripping open pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge its border. The LORD vows fire on Rabbah's wall to devour palaces amid battle shouting and storm, and the king and princes will go into captivity together.

l: coming judgment, The Book of Amos
s: affects warriors (the swift, strong, mighty) [they cannot escape or deliver themselves] The judgment takes the form of fire on Moab and Judah and of crushing on Israel like a cart full of grain. For Israel, flight will fail the swift, the strong and mighty cannot save themselves, the archer will not stand, the fast runner and horseman will not escape, and even the courageous will flee naked on that day.

Punishment is announced for each nation with the formula 'for three transgressions, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment.' It takes the form of fire devouring palaces, along with captivity and the cutting off of rulers and inhabitants.

Moab is condemned for burning the Edomite king's bones into lime. The LORD will send fire to devour Kerioth's palaces, and Moab will die amid tumult, shouting and trumpets, its judge and princes killed.

l: the needy and poor (oppressed by Israel's merchants), The Book of Amos
s: The needy and poor are the ones whom the merchants desire to swallow up and cause to fail. They are bought for silver and for a pair of sandals, and are the object of the deceit the LORD swears never to forget.

l: prophets (raised from Israel's sons), The Book of Amos
s: is_a servants of the Lord GOD The prophets are called the LORD's servants, to whom the Lord GOD reveals His secret before doing anything. Having heard the LORD speak like a roaring lion, the passage says they cannot help but prophesy.

l: Israel's transgressions and oppression of the poor, The Book of Amos
s: includes the righteous and the needy (Israel's victims) [trampling the poor and denying justice] Israel is accused of selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, trampling the heads of the poor into the dust, and denying justice to the oppressed. A man and his father use the same maiden, profaning the LORD's holy name. They lie beside altars on garments taken in pledge and drink wine of those who have been fined in the house of their God.

Samaria is a mountainous place marked by unrest and oppression. Its elites feel secure on the mountain and hoard plunder in palaces. Ashdod and Egypt are summoned to witness its wrongdoing. Its comfortable are barely rescued, and the LORD will deliver up the city, striking down its houses, great and little.
Bethel is a king's sanctuary and royal house that Israel is told not to seek; the LORD declares it will come to nothing, with unquenchable fire threatened.

l: adversary (against Israel), The Book of Amos
s: will_overrun the land [will pull down strongholds and plunder fortresses] An adversary is announced as coming to overrun the land. He will pull down the strongholds of Samaria's people and plunder their fortresses.

l: Israel's sins and oppression, The Book of Amos
s: The text names Israel's sins as the reason for punishment, citing unrest and oppression in Samaria. The LORD says the people do not know to do right and hoard plunder and loot in their palaces, and He also refers to the transgressions of Israel and the altars of Bethel.

l: coming punishment and destruction, The Book of Amos
s: A day of divine reckoning for Israel's transgressions: the LORD brings an adversary who overruns the land, topples strongholds and plunders fortresses, rescuing only a scrap-like remnant. Bethel's altar horns are cut off and fall, then winter, summer, ivory and great houses are struck down and end.

l: cows of Bashan, The Book of Amos
s: The cows of Bashan, on Samaria's mountain, habitually oppress the poor and crush the needy while ordering their husbands to bring drinks. They are warned that days will come when they are dragged off with hooks, exiting through wall breaches straight ahead, and cast into Harmon.
will_go_into captivity Gilgal is named with Bethel and Beersheba as a place Israel must not seek, enter, or pass to. The LORD declares it will surely go into captivity.

l: deportation with hooks, The Book of Amos
s: A sworn prophecy by the Lord GOD of coming days when the cows of Bashan are dragged away with hooks, the last with fish hooks, exiting through wall breaches and casting themselves into Harmon.

l: calamities sent against Israel, The Book of Amos
s: A series of calamities the LORD declares he sent against Israel: famine, selective drought, blight, locusts, Egypt-like plagues, slaughter of young men, and a Sodom-and-Gomorrah overthrow. Escalating from hunger and withheld rain to death and destruction, it ends with survivors like a burning stick plucked from fire.

l: failure to return to the LORD, The Book of Amos
s: After each calamity the LORD repeats that Israel has not returned to him, a refrain appearing in verses 6 through 11. Because of this, he tells Israel to prepare to meet its God.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Amos
s: The house of Israel is a collective people, lamented as fallen and called small, whose fate unfolds across three chapters. It is first mourned in a lament, with its cities to be reduced to a tenth of their fighting men. It is accused of trampling the poor, taking bribes, hating the one who reproves in the gate, and turning justice to wormwood. It owns houses of cut stone and vineyards it will not enjoy, and it made idols. It is urged to seek good and establish justice so the LORD may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph. Punishment includes wailing, captivity beyond Damascus, and a nation raised against it. Finally, Jacob, described by Amos as small, pleads, and the LORD relents from the locusts and the fire.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Amos
s: is darkness [not light] The day of the LORD is something Israel desires, but the LORD pronounces woe on those who long for it. He says it is darkness and not light, comparing it to a man who flees a lion and meets a bear, or leans on a wall at home and is bitten by a snake.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Amos
s: is_to_be_established in the courts [commanded] Justice is turned to wormwood by those who cast righteousness to the earth, and it is denied in the courts through bribes and the rejection of the needy. The LORD commands Israel to establish justice in the courts and to let it roll on like rivers and righteousness like a mighty stream.

l: religious feasts and offerings, The Book of Amos
s: The LORD says he hates and despises Israel's feasts and solemn assemblies. He will not accept their burnt offerings, meal offerings, or peace offerings, and he tells them to take away the noise of their songs and harps.
Captivity is announced as the coming fate of Gilgal and of Israel. The LORD says he will cause the people to go into captivity beyond Damascus.

l: complacent elites (notable men of Zion and Samaria), The Book of Amos
s: These are notable men of the chief of the nations, living at ease in Zion and secure in Samaria. They recline on ivory beds, eat choice lambs and calves, drink wine from bowls, anoint themselves with the best oils, and invent musical instruments like David. They are not grieved by Joseph's affliction, push away the evil day, boast of their own strength, and turn justice into poison. They are told they will go captive among the first, ending their feasting.

l: nation (raised up against Israel), The Book of Amos
s: afflicts house of Israel [from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah] An unnamed nation is to be raised up by the LORD against the house of Israel. It will afflict Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.

l: captivity (of Israel), The Book of Amos
s: Israel's captivity, prophesied by Amos, is foretold in Chapter 6: notable men will go captive first, ending their feasting and lounging, alongside deaths in houses and affliction by a raised-up nation.

Amaziah is the priest of Bethel who reports Amos to Jeroboam as a conspirator and orders him to flee to Judah. In response, Amos pronounces judgment: Amaziah's wife will become a prostitute, his children will die by sword, and he will die in an unclean land.

formed_by Lord GOD [at the beginning of the latter growth] In the first vision the LORD forms locusts at the start of the latter growth, after the king's harvest. They finish eating the grass of the land, prompting Amos's plea, and the LORD relents.

l: fire (judgment by fire), The Book of Amos
s: dried_up great deep In the second vision the Lord GOD calls for judgment by fire, which dries up the great deep and would have devoured the land. After Amos pleads, the LORD relents and says it shall not be.

l: plumb line, The Book of Amos
s: is_held_by Lord GOD [seen in his hand beside a wall] In the third vision the Lord stands beside a wall made by a plumb line with a plumb line in his hand. He tells Amos he will set a plumb line in the middle of Israel and will not pass by them again, with desolation to follow.

l: basket of summer fruit (Amos's vision), The Book of Amos
s: symbolizes coming end and judgment on Israel [interpretation given by the LORD] The basket of summer fruit is what the Lord GOD shows Amos and what Amos names when asked what he sees. It serves as the sign that the end has come on Israel.

l: exploitative merchants (addressed by Amos), The Book of Amos
s: Israel's merchants habitually oppress and swallow up the needy and poor. They resent the Sabbath and new moon because it delays selling wheat, cheat with a small ephah, large shekel and deceitful balances, buy the poor for silver and sandals, and sell sweepings. The LORD swears never to forget their works.

l: famine of hearing the LORD's words, The Book of Amos
s: A spiritual famine announced by the LORD, not of bread or water but of hearing his words. People wander from sea to sea and north to east seeking his word without finding it, and beautiful virgins and young men faint from thirst.

l: coming end and judgment on Israel, The Book of Amos
s: is_a final judgment [the LORD will not pass by them again] The judgment is signaled by the basket of summer fruit and the declaration that the end has come. It includes the land trembling, the sun going down at noon, the earth darkened in clear day, feasts turned to mourning with sackcloth and baldness, and a bitter day like mourning for an only son.

l: dishonest trade practices, The Book of Amos
s: The text describes making the ephah small, the shekel large, and dealing falsely with balances of deceit. It also includes selling the sweepings with the wheat and treating the Sabbath and new moon as obstacles to marketing grain. The LORD swears he will never forget such works.

l: sinners of my people, The Book of Amos
s: Sinners among the Lord's people, who complacently claim evil will never overtake them, are declared by the Lord to all die by the sword.

l: tent of David, The Book of Amos
s: The tent of David is a fallen structure with breaches and ruins; the Lord promises to raise it, close its breaches, and rebuild it as in old days, so they possess Edom's remnant and the nations.

l: restoration of Israel, The Book of Amos
s: Restoration of Israel is the Lord's promise to return his people from captivity amid abundant harvests, where they rebuild ruined cities, plant vineyards and gardens, and settle permanently on their land, never again being plucked up from it.
